title: grant proposal|a community oral-history project for a public library
text:
The Riverfront Public Library requests $42,500 from the Community Heritage Foundation to launch “Voices of the Riverfront: Kingfisher Neighborhood Oral Histories,” a twelve-month community documentation initiative. The project will capture the stories of long-time residents of the Kingfisher neighborhood, a once-thriving industrial corridor along the Blackwater River that has seen decades of economic change, flooding, and redevelopment. These first-person accounts are at risk of being lost as the neighborhood’s older population ages and younger residents move away.

Library director Patricia Morrow and archives supervisor David Park will oversee the project in partnership with the Kingfisher Neighborhood Association and the East Side Senior Center. Dr. Naomi Okonkwo, a public historian at Baldwin State University, will serve as project scholar, training volunteers in ethical interview techniques and helping place individual stories within broader regional history. James “Jimmy” Alvarez, a retired steelworker and neighborhood association president, and Sister Mary Clare O’Donnell, who has run the senior center’s meals program since 1998, will recruit narrators and advise the team on culturally sensitive outreach.

Between February and August 2026, project staff and trained volunteers will conduct forty audio interviews, each lasting sixty to ninety minutes. Interviews will be recorded on Tascam DR-40X digital recorders and backed up to encrypted drives stored at the library. All narrators will sign release forms approved by the library’s legal counsel, with options for embargoed access when requested. Verbal Ink will transcribe the recordings verbatim at a cost of $9,000, and David Park will apply standardized metadata so the collection is searchable by name, place, occupation, and subject.

The finished collection will be deposited in the library’s Southwest Ohio Digital History Archive and made freely available by November 1, 2026. A project website, designed by local firm Mayfly Digital, will stream selected excerpts alongside photographs and scanned documents contributed by participants. Three public listening events will follow: a launch reception at the Kingfisher branch on October 15, 2026; a high school workshop led by Dr. Okonkwo on November 5, 2026; and a community showcase at the East Side Senior Center on December 3, 2026. Each event will include a brief oral-history training so attendees can continue recording family stories on their own.

The total project budget is $42,500. We are requesting $30,000 from the foundation. The remaining $12,500 will come from the library’s Friends group ($7,500) and a city cultural preservation grant ($5,000). Funds will cover part-time project coordination ($8,000), transcription ($9,000), equipment ($4,500), community liaison stipends ($4,500), website development ($6,000), event costs ($3,000), and archival supplies and metadata work ($7,500).

“Voices of the Riverfront” will give Kingfisher residents authority over their own history, create a permanent research resource, and offer a replicable model for other neighborhoods served by the library. We welcome the opportunity to discuss the project further and can provide letters of support from Dr. Okonkwo, Mr. Alvarez, and Sister O’Donnell upon request.

title: government audit report|oversight of veterans' disability claim processing times
text:
Oversight of Disability Claim Processing Times Remains Inadequate

 Findings

The Department of Veterans Affairs has made measurable progress in reducing the average time required to adjudicate disability compensation claims. Since fiscal year 2019, the Veterans Benefits Administration reports that the average number of days to complete a claim has fallen from 127 to approximately 104. Yet this headline figure obscures persistent weaknesses in how the department monitors, verifies, and addresses processing delays across its 56 regional offices. Our review found that the VBA’s oversight framework relies on self-reported data that is inconsistently validated, uses performance targets that do not fully reflect veterans’ experiences, and lacks sufficient mechanisms to identify and correct regional disparities.

At the centre of the problem is the department’s reliance on the Veterans Service Network, the case-management system that regional offices use to record claim statuses and completion dates. While the system produces the aggregate statistics that the VBA reports to Congress and the public, our audit determined that it does not adequately capture the time a claim spends awaiting action outside a regional office’s direct control. When a claim is transferred between offices, sent for a medical examination, or held for additional evidence, the elapsed days are often excluded from the office’s processing-time calculation. As a result, the averages reported to headquarters can understate the actual time veterans wait by several weeks. In a sample of 340 claims completed between October 2022 and March 2023, we found that 27 percent had intervals of 30 days or more that were not reflected in the office-level processing metric.

Compounding this issue, the VBA’s quality-review process does not routinely test whether regional offices are accurately recording claim milestones. Quality-review teams examine a small sample of completed claims for adjudicative accuracy, but they do not independently verify the dates entered into the system or assess whether delays were properly classified. Without such verification, headquarters cannot reliably distinguish between offices that process claims efficiently and those that merely record them efficiently.

Regional variation in performance further illustrates the limits of current oversight. In fiscal year 2023, the percentage of claims taking more than 125 days ranged from 11 percent at the highest-performing regional office to 38 percent at the lowest. The VBA’s national average masks this spread and, consequently, the concentration of delay among certain veteran populations. Offices with larger backlogs, higher proportions of complex claims, or staffing shortfalls were not consistently identified for targeted intervention until delays had already become severe. The VBA has established a national initiative to redistribute inventory, but its criteria for selecting offices for assistance are based in part on the same self-reported data whose accuracy our audit questions.

We also found that the VBA’s public reporting does not include information on how long veterans wait for required medical examinations or on the time required to resolve appeals of initial decisions. These periods can add months or years to the overall process, yet they are largely absent from the department’s quarterly performance briefings. The omission limits the ability of Congress, veterans’ service organisations, and the public to assess whether improvements in initial claims handling are translating into faster final resolution.

 Recommendations

To strengthen oversight of disability claim processing times, we recommend that the Under Secretary for Benefits take three actions. First, the VBA should revise its performance metrics to account for the full duration of a claim, including time spent awaiting transfers, examinations, and development actions, and it should report these figures to Congress alongside the existing office-level averages. Second, the department should expand quality-review procedures to include independent verification of claim-status dates and classification of delays, with findings reported to regional directors and senior leadership. Third, the VBA should publish supplementary data on examination wait times and appeals duration in its quarterly reports, and it should develop a risk-based process to identify underperforming regional offices before backlogs accumulate.

The Department of Veterans Affairs concurred with all three recommendations and outlined planned corrective actions, which we will monitor until fully implemented.

title: legal memorandum|whether a non-compete clause is enforceable under state law
text:
To: Senior Partner
From: Associate Attorney
Date: October 15, 2024
Re: Enforceability of Non-Compete Clause Under State Law

QUESTION PRESENTED

Whether a non-compete covenant contained in an employment agreement is enforceable against a former employee under applicable state law.

BRIEF ANSWER

Probably yes, provided the restriction is reasonable in geographic scope, duration, and subject matter and is necessary to protect a legitimate business interest. However, the precise outcome depends significantly on the governing state jurisdiction, as states vary widely in their treatment of non-compete agreements.

STATEMENT OF FACTS

Our client, a technology firm, seeks to enforce a non-compete clause against a former employee who recently joined a direct competitor. The agreement prohibits the employee from working for any competitor within a fifty-mile radius for a period of twelve months. The client asserts that the former employee had access to confidential proprietary information and trade secrets during the course of his employment.

DISCUSSION

The majority of jurisdictions evaluate non-compete agreements under a reasonableness standard. Courts generally enforce such covenants only if they are supported by adequate consideration, necessary to protect a legitimate business interest, reasonable in duration, reasonable in geographic scope, and not unduly harsh or oppressive to the employee or contrary to public policy. Mere protection against ordinary competition is typically insufficient; the employer must demonstrate a protectable interest such as trade secrets, confidential business information, or established customer relationships.

Assuming the applicable state follows the majority approach, the covenant here warrants careful scrutiny. The twelve-month duration is frequently upheld in many states, though courts in industries characterized by rapid technological change may find such a period excessive. The fifty-mile geographic restriction presents a closer question. Its enforceability depends largely upon the employer’s actual business footprint. If the company regularly markets its products or services throughout that radius, the limitation may be deemed reasonable. Conversely, if the employer’s operations are purely local, a court may find the restriction overbroad and decline to enforce it.

State law variations complicate this analysis considerably. Several jurisdictions, notably California, North Dakota, and Oklahoma, statutorily prohibit post-employment non-compete agreements for employees absent narrow exceptions, such as those connected to the sale of a business. Other states apply a blue-pencil doctrine, permitting courts to sever offensive or overbroad provisions while enforcing the remaining reasonable terms. Certain jurisdictions reject blue-penciling entirely and will invalidate the covenant if any portion is overbroad. Furthermore, recent legislative trends in numerous states have introduced income-based thresholds, advance notice requirements, and garden-leave provisions, each of which may independently affect enforceability.

Given these distinctions, the client’s likelihood of success hinges primarily upon identifying the governing state law. If the applicable jurisdiction adheres to a traditional reasonableness analysis and the restriction is narrowly tailored to prevent disclosure of confidential information, a court will likely enforce the agreement or modify it to comply with legal standards. If the jurisdiction disfavors such covenants, enforcement becomes considerably more difficult.

CONCLUSION

The non-compete clause is likely enforceable if the applicable state applies a reasonableness standard and the restriction is appropriately tailored to protect legitimate business interests. We should promptly determine the governing state law and verify that the geographic and temporal limitations reflect the company’s actual operational needs. Should the applicable law prove hostile to non-competes, we should consider alternative protective measures, including robust confidentiality and non-solicitation agreements.

Lundgren's Food Markets, Inc.
Eau Claire, Wisconsin
March 14, 2026

Dear Fellow Shareholders,

We opened nine stores in fiscal 2025, and I won't pretend every one of them went smoothly. More on that below. First, the year itself.

Fiscal 2025, the 52 weeks ended January 31, 2026, was the biggest growth year in our 63-year history. Net sales reached $1.14 billion, up 11.3%. Comparable-store sales rose 3.8%. Net income was $31.6 million, or $1.87 per diluted share, compared with $26.9 million, or $1.62, a year earlier. We finished the year with 47 stores, up from 38, and for the first time that count includes Iowa.

Iowa mattered to us. On March 12, we opened in Decorah, a town of 7,500 that had been without a full-service grocer for two years. The store did $312,000 its first week, the strongest opening we've ever had, and it hasn't slowed. Waukon followed in June and Oelwein in September; all three are ahead of plan. We also added fill-in stores in Hudson, Wisconsin, and Woodbury, Minnesota.

In May, we acquired four former Feldmann's Market locations in the Twin Cities suburbs when the Feldmann family chose to retire. Converting someone else's store is harder than building your own. The Maplewood conversion took eleven weeks instead of seven and cost us roughly $400,000 in lost sales. I consider that tuition. The four stores are now collectively comping above 6%.

Behind all of it sits the supply chain. In October, we opened our 420,000-square-foot distribution center in Menomonie, Wisconsin, a $58 million project completed on schedule and $2 million under budget. It can support 65 stores before we need another. Capital spending for the year totaled $94 million, funded almost entirely from operating cash flow; long-term debt stands at $61 million.

Our people did the actual work. We raised starting pay to $15.50 an hour in April, promoted 214 employees into management, and cut store-manager turnover to 11%, the lowest since 2019. If you visit Decorah, say hello to Donna Reilly, who started bagging groceries in La Crosse in 1988 and now runs the best new store we have.

Now the honest part. The Rochester remodel ran nine weeks late. Shrink reached 3.1% of sales, and we were slow to act on self-checkout losses. A national discounter opened across from our Albert Lea store in August, and that store's comps fell 4% in the fourth quarter. We're answering with lower prices on 600 everyday items, not with gimmicks.

For fiscal 2026, we plan five new stores, including our first in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, plus six remodels. The Board has raised the quarterly dividend to $0.14 per share, our ninth straight annual increase.

My grandfather opened a 6,000-square-foot store in Eau Claire in 1962 with a borrowed truck and a fear of debt I have inherited only partially. He would have enjoyed this year. Thank you for your investment, and for your patience in the stretches when we earn it less than we'd like.

Sincerely,

Margaret Lundgren
President and Chief Executive Officer

title: legal memorandum|whether a non-compete clause is enforceable under state law
text:
II. Analysis: Enforceability of the Non-Compete Covenant

The threshold question is whether the non-compete clause is enforceable as a matter of state law. In most jurisdictions, courts will enforce a non-compete agreement only if it is: (1) supported by adequate consideration; (2) necessary to protect a legitimate business interest; and (3) reasonable in scope, duration, and geographic reach. The burden of establishing each element rests on the party seeking enforcement, and courts scrutinize these agreements with particular care because they operate as restraints on trade and limit an individual’s ability to earn a livelihood.

A. Consideration

For a non-compete clause to be binding, it must be supported by consideration that is distinct from continued at-will employment if the covenant is entered into after the employment relationship has begun. Mere continuation of employment—without a promise of additional compensation, promotion, training, access to confidential information, or some other material benefit—is generally insufficient to support a new restrictive covenant. If, however, the non-compete was part of the initial offer of employment or was tied to the sale of a business, goodwill, or a separate economic benefit, courts are more likely to find adequate consideration. Here, the timing and context of the agreement’s execution will therefore be determinative.

B. Legitimate Business Interest

Even with adequate consideration, a non-compete cannot be enforced as a general prohibition on competition. It must protect an identifiable legitimate business interest. Recognized interests typically include trade secrets, confidential business information, customer relationships developed at the employer’s expense, specialized training, and goodwill associated with the sale of a business. Courts distinguish between genuine protectable interests and ordinary competitive advantages or skills an employee acquired through general experience. A non-compete that merely prevents an employee from using general knowledge, skill, or industry contacts is likely to be deemed overbroad and unenforceable.

C. Reasonableness of Restriction

The core of the analysis is whether the covenant is reasonable in light of the interest asserted. Courts evaluate three interrelated factors: duration, geographic scope, and the scope of prohibited activity. The restriction must be no broader than necessary to protect the employer’s legitimate interest. A temporal limitation of six months to two years is often upheld in the employment context, while longer periods are viewed with increasing skepticism unless supported by special circumstances, such as the sale of a business. Geographic scope is reasonable when it corresponds to the employee’s actual territory or the market the employer actually serves; a nationwide restriction for a locally operating business is ordinarily excessive. Likewise, the covenant should not bar the employee from performing work wholly unrelated to the employee’s prior duties.

Many states apply a “blue-pencil” doctrine, under which a court may modify an overbroad covenant by striking or narrowing offending language rather than invalidating the agreement entirely. Other jurisdictions reject blue-penciling and will refuse to enforce an overbroad covenant altogether, on the theory that an employer should not benefit from drafting an unreasonably broad restriction. The applicable state’s approach to severability is therefore critical.

D. Public Policy and Statutory Limitations

State legislatures have increasingly restricted non-compete agreements. Some states categorically prohibit them for low-wage workers or impose minimum income thresholds; others require advance notice, post-termination garden leave, or impose heightened scrutiny on non-competes in specific industries such as healthcare or broadcasting. In addition, many states enforce a strong public policy against restraints on trade and will construe ambiguous language against the drafter. Any statutory prohibition or regulatory guidance in the governing state may be outcome-determinative.

E. Conclusion

Assuming the agreement is supported by adequate consideration and the employer can demonstrate a legitimate business interest, the covenant’s enforceability will turn on whether its temporal, geographic, and functional limitations are narrowly tailored. If the restriction is substantially broader than necessary to protect that interest, a court may either decline to enforce it or blue-pencil it to a permissible scope, depending on the state. Before finalizing litigation strategy, it is essential to confirm the governing state’s particular common-law and statutory framework.

text:
The National Central Bank left its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Thursday, opting to keep borrowing costs steady as inflation continues to ease toward the institution’s long-term target.

Policymakers voted to maintain the overnight lending rate at 5.25 percent, a level it has held for three consecutive meetings, citing progress in bringing price growth under control without tipping the economy into a sharper slowdown. The decision was widely expected by financial markets, though investors parsed the bank’s statement for clues about when officials might begin to lower rates.

Consumer price inflation slowed to 2.8 percent in October on an annual basis, down from a peak of 7.2 percent in late 2022 and now within half a percentage point of the central bank’s 2 percent goal. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, also moderated to 3.1 percent, suggesting that underlying price pressures are gradually unwinding after more than two years of aggressive monetary tightening.

In its post-meeting statement, the central bank said that while inflation has declined faster than anticipated over recent months, it remains too early to declare victory. Officials reiterated that policy will need to stay “sufficiently restrictive for some time” to ensure that inflation returns to target on a sustained basis.

“Recent data are encouraging, but the path ahead is uncertain,” Governor Elena Marquez said at a news conference following the decision. “We have made substantial progress, and the economy has proven more resilient than many forecasters expected. Still, we want to see more evidence that inflation is convincingly moving back to 2 percent before we consider adjusting our policy stance.”

The bank’s decision reflects a delicate balancing act. On one side, officials are wary of cutting rates too soon and allowing inflation to reaccelerate, as happened during previous episodes in the 1970s and early 1980s. On the other, keeping rates elevated for too long risks deepening a slowdown in manufacturing, housing, and business investment, where higher borrowing costs have already begun to bite.

Economic growth has cooled noticeably over the past year. Gross domestic product expanded at an annualized rate of 1.2 percent in the third quarter, down from 2.9 percent in the same period a year earlier. The labor market, while still robust by historical standards, has shown signs of loosening, with job openings declining and wage growth slowing from its post-pandemic highs.

Financial markets had priced in a roughly 90 percent probability that the central bank would hold rates steady this week, with the first quarter-point rate cut now expected by mid-next year. Government bond yields edged lower following the announcement, while the domestic currency weakened slightly against the dollar as traders interpreted the bank’s tone as slightly less hawkish than in previous months.

Analysts said the statement removed some of the more forceful language about future tightening, a signal that policymakers believe the most intense phase of rate increases is over. The bank’s previous statement had said it was “prepared to raise rates further if appropriate,” whereas Thursday’s version noted only that officials would “continue to assess incoming data and the evolving outlook.”

“That subtle change matters,” said David Chen, chief economist at Meridian Capital. “It tells you the central bank is comfortable where it is and is moving into a holding pattern. They are no longer actively thinking about hiking, but they are also not ready to cut. The next move is almost certainly down, but the timing depends on whether inflation keeps falling.”

Households and businesses have begun to feel relief from the rapid price increases that eroded purchasing power over the past two years. Grocery prices have stabilized, gasoline costs have retreated from their highs, and supply-chain disruptions that fueled inflation during the pandemic have largely normalized.

Still, shelter costs remain elevated, and services inflation has proven sticky, driven in part by wage growth in sectors such as healthcare, education, and hospitality. Central bank officials said they are watching those categories closely.

The bank also published updated economic projections showing inflation reaching its 2 percent target by the second half of next year, slightly sooner than it had forecast three months ago. It lowered its projection for economic growth in 2024 and 2025 and raised its unemployment rate forecast modestly, reflecting the lagged effects of tighter monetary policy.

Governor Marquez declined to commit to a specific timeline for rate cuts, repeating that future decisions would be made “meeting by meeting” based on the totality of incoming data. She stressed that the central bank would remain patient to avoid undermining the progress made so far.

“We understand that higher interest rates create hardship for borrowers and for the economy more broadly,” she said. “But the cost of failing to restore price stability would be far greater. Our commitment is to bring inflation back to target and keep it there.”

The central bank’s next policy meeting is scheduled for late January.

title: government audit report|delays and cost overruns in a federal broadband grant program
text:
OFFICE OF INSPECTOR GENERAL  
U.S. DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE  

Audit of the Rural Broadband Infrastructure Initiative: Program Delays and Cost Overruns  
Report No. OIG-24-036  
September 14, 2023  

The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) awarded $4.2 billion in RBII grants between March 2021 and December 2022 to extend high-speed internet access to unserved communities across fourteen states. Our audit, which examined disbursements through June 2023, found that the program has fallen substantially behind schedule and faces cost escalations that threaten its statutory mandate to connect 2.4 million households by December 2025.

Only 18 percent of funded projects have broken ground, and NTIA officials now acknowledge that the original completion timeline is "unachievable." In Montana, the Big Sky Fiber Consortium received $287 million in September 2021 to build 4,200 miles of middle-mile infrastructure. As of March 2023, the consortium had laid just 612 miles. Project managers cited permitting backlogs at the Bureau of Land Management and a 340 percent spike in fiber-optic cable prices following pandemic-era supply constraints. The Montana project, originally budgeted at $412 million when matching funds are included, is now projected to cost $611 million—a $199 million overrun that state regulators have not yet reconciled with NTIA.

Similar patterns emerged in Appalachia. The Kentucky Mountain Communications District, awarded $156 million in January 2022, submitted revised engineering surveys in October 2022 that added $47 million to its construction estimate. The increase stemmed from underestimated rock-boring requirements in Powell and Wolfe Counties, where limestone geology added an average of $28,000 per mile to burial costs. NTIA approved the amendment without requiring independent validation of the new estimates, despite the agency’s own guidance calling for third-party engineering reviews on adjustments exceeding 15 percent of total award value.

Labor shortages compounded these delays. Contractors in Mississippi and Alabama reported that specialized fusion splicer technicians, who commanded $34 per hour in 2020, now require $58 per hour plus per diem. Three prime contractors—Lindell Communications, Southern Broadband Solutions, and Tri-State Utility Constructors—collectively missed 14 of 22 milestone deadlines tied to reimbursement eligibility. NTIA program officer Patricia Okonkwo testified before our auditors that the agency lacked the staffing to monitor construction sites in person and had relied on self-certified progress reports from recipients.

The mapping data used to prioritize awards also proved unreliable. Our review of FCC broadband maps from December 2020—the foundation for RBII eligibility determinations—identified 87,000 locations in Louisiana and Arkansas that were incorrectly classified as unserved. NTIA obligated $93 million to serve those addresses before updated maps, released in November 2022, revealed existing cable or fixed wireless coverage. The agency has recouped only $11 million of those funds.

We recommend that NTIA suspend disbursement on projects exhibiting cost variances above 10 percent until recipients submit verified engineering assessments. The agency should also renegotiate the December 2025 service deadline with Congress and establish a dedicated unit to validate contractor milestone claims against geospatial construction data. NTIA concurred with four of our six recommendations.

title: medical patient information leaflet|managing type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise
text:
Managing your diabetes with diet and exercise

For most people with type 2 diabetes, changes to eating and physical activity are the foundation of treatment — not an optional extra. A healthier lifestyle lowers blood glucose (sugar), improves blood pressure and cholesterol, and can reduce the amount of medicine you need. In some people, substantial and sustained weight loss can bring blood sugar back to normal without medication. This is called remission. It does not happen for everyone, and it is not a cure, but every improvement in diet and activity brings real benefits.

 Eating well

There is no special "diabetic diet". The healthy eating advice that applies to everyone applies to you — it simply matters more.

- Build your plate around vegetables and salad. Aim for roughly half the plate, with a quarter for starchy carbohydrates and a quarter for protein such as fish, eggs, beans or lean meat.
- Choose high-fibre carbohydrates. Wholemeal bread, brown rice, wholewheat pasta and oats release glucose more slowly than white or refined versions, so blood sugar rises more gently.
- Cut down on sugar. Sugary drinks are the single easiest target — swap them for water or sugar-free alternatives. Ordinary fruit juice and smoothies should be limited to one small glass (150 ml) a day, with a meal. Whole fruit is fine in moderation.
- Limit saturated fat and salt. Go easy on fatty meat, butter, pastries and fried food, and keep salt below 6 g a day to protect your heart and blood pressure.
- Avoid "diabetic" foods. They are expensive, still affect your weight and blood sugar, and can have a laxative effect.

If you are overweight, losing 5–10 per cent of your body weight will noticeably improve your blood sugar control. Slow, steady loss — around half a kilogram a week — is safest and most likely to last.

 Alcohol

You do not have to give up alcohol, but keep within recommended limits. Alcohol is high in calories and, if you take insulin or tablets called sulfonylureas, it can cause low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia, or a "hypo") many hours later. Never drink on an empty stomach.

 Being active

Aim for at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity — brisk walking, cycling or swimming, at a pace where you can talk but not sing. This can be broken into sessions of ten minutes or more spread across the week. On two or more days, add activities that strengthen your muscles, such as carrying shopping, heavy gardening or using resistance bands. Try to break up long periods of sitting with a few minutes of light movement every half hour; even a short walk after meals helps to flatten blood sugar rises.

If you are not used to exercise, build up gradually and choose activities you enjoy. Wear well-fitting shoes and check your feet afterwards, as diabetes can reduce sensation and slow healing. If you take insulin or sulfonylureas, exercise can trigger hypos, so carry glucose tablets or a sugary drink, and speak to your care team before making major changes to your routine.

 Making changes stick

Set small, specific goals rather than overhauling everything at once. Plan meals, shop from a list, and involve your household — healthy eating benefits everyone. Ask your GP or diabetes nurse about structured education courses, which are proven to help. Do not aim for perfection; a lapse is not a failure.

 When to seek advice

Contact your GP or diabetes care team if you have symptoms of high blood sugar — unusual thirst, passing urine frequently, tiredness or blurred vision — or if you are having frequent hypos. Attend all your regular reviews, including blood tests, foot checks and eye screening: they catch problems early, when they are easiest to treat.

WASHINGTON — The country’s central bank left its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Wednesday, extending a pause that began earlier this year as policymakers weighed steadily slowing inflation against still-healthy consumer spending and a tight labor market.

The monetary policy committee voted unanimously to hold the overnight lending rate at 5.25 percent, where it has stood since a final quarter-point increase in July. In a brief statement, the bank said recent data showed inflation continuing to moderate but emphasized that price growth remained above its long-run 2 percent target.

“Inflation has moved lower over recent months, supported by easing supply-chain disruptions and softer energy prices,” the central bank said. “The committee remains highly attentive to inflation risks and will continue to monitor the implications of incoming information for the economic outlook.”

The decision was widely expected by financial markets and most economists, who have been watching for signs that a string of aggressive rate increases over the past two years is finally cooling demand without tipping the economy into recession. Consumer price inflation slowed to 3.2 percent in June on an annual basis, down sharply from a peak of 9.1 percent in the summer of 2022 and below the 4 percent recorded in May. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, also eased, though it remained elevated at 4.8 percent.

Policymakers noted that the economy has continued to expand at a “moderate pace,” supported by robust household spending. At the same time, they acknowledged that the labor market, while still strong by historical standards, is showing signs of rebalancing. Job openings have declined from record highs, and wage growth has gradually slowed.

Central bank Chair Elena Voss told reporters after the decision that officials were encouraged by the progress on inflation but were not yet ready to declare victory. “We have a long way to go to restore price stability,” Voss said. “Our policy stance is restrictive, and we believe it is having the intended effect. But we will need to see more evidence that inflation is moving down sustainably toward our target before considering any reduction in rates.”

The bank also reiterated that it would be prepared to adjust monetary policy if new risks emerged that could impede progress toward its goals. That language left the door open to another rate increase later this year if inflation proves more persistent than expected.

Financial markets barely moved on the announcement, with stocks holding near earlier levels and government bond yields ticking lower. Investors have increasingly bet that the central bank has reached the end of its tightening cycle, though expectations for the timing of rate cuts remain divided. Futures markets are pricing in the possibility of one additional quarter-point hike before the end of the year, with the first rate cut potentially coming next spring.

Economists said the decision reflected a careful balancing act. “The central bank is trying to avoid over-tightening now that inflation is clearly decelerating,” said Marcus Chen, chief economist at Horizon Research. “But it also wants to keep financial conditions tight enough to prevent a rebound in price pressures. Holding steady is the right move at this stage.”

Some analysts cautioned that the path back to 2 percent inflation could be bumpy. Housing costs remain high, and services inflation has proven stubborn. Global oil prices have also risen in recent weeks, raising the possibility that headline inflation could tick higher again in the near term.

The central bank’s next policy meeting is scheduled for late September, when officials will have two more months of inflation, employment, and growth data to consider. In the meantime, Voss said policymakers would remain “data dependent” and would not hesitate to act if economic conditions changed materially.

For consumers and businesses, the steady rate decision means borrowing costs are likely to stay elevated for the foreseeable future. Mortgage rates, auto loans, and corporate debt are all expected to remain expensive by historical standards, even as inflation gradually loses steam.

The central bank also released updated economic projections showing that officials expect inflation to fall to 2.5 percent by the end of next year before reaching the 2 percent target in 2026. The unemployment rate is forecast to edge up slightly to 4.2 percent by the end of 2024, reflecting a modest cooling in labor demand.

With price pressures easing and the economy proving more resilient than many had feared, policymakers appear content to wait and see whether the most aggressive rate-hiking campaign in decades has done enough to return inflation to normal.

title: travel guide|two days in Lisbon on a budget
text:
Two Days in Lisbon on a Budget

Lisbon is one of Europe’s most captivating capitals, and it is entirely possible to explore its historic neighbourhoods, iconic viewpoints, and distinctive cuisine without spending a fortune. With careful planning, two full days can provide a rich introduction to the city while keeping daily expenses modest.

Day One: Belém and Alfama

Begin your morning in Belém, a riverside district famous for its monuments to Portugal’s Age of Discovery. Take the tram or bus from the city centre; a 24-hour public transport ticket offers excellent value and covers trams, buses, and the metro. Many visitors arrive early to see the Belém Tower and the Monument to the Discoveries from the outside, which is free. While the interiors charge admission, walking along the waterfront and photographing these limestone landmarks costs nothing. A custard tart and coffee at the historic Pastéis de Belém bakery can be enjoyed economically if shared.

Next, visit the Jerónimos Monastery. Entry is free on the first Sunday morning of each month, and students or seniors may receive reduced rates. Even if you do not enter, the southern portal and adjacent gardens are impressive.

Return to the centre by early afternoon and head to Alfama, Lisbon’s oldest quarter. Wander through its narrow cobblestone streets, whitewashed houses, and small squares. Climb towards São Jorge Castle; the castle grounds require a ticket, but the surrounding Miradouro da Senhora do Monte and Miradouro da Graça offer sweeping views for free. These miradouros are ideal places to watch the late afternoon light turn the terracotta rooftops golden.

For dinner, avoid the tourist traps near the castle. Instead, choose a tasca, a traditional tavern, in Alfama or Graça, where a daily set menu often includes soup, main course, dessert, and wine for under twelve euros.

Day Two: Baixa, Chiado, and Modern Lisbon

Start at Praça do Comércio, the grand riverside square rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake. From there, stroll up Rua Augusta, a pedestrian thoroughfare lined with shops and cafés, until you reach the triumphal arch. You can admire the architecture without entering paid attractions. Continue to Rossio and the Elevador de Santa Justa. Rather than paying the tourist fare, walk up the adjacent hill to the Carmo Convent ruins, or simply view the elevator from the street.

In Chiado, browse the historic cafés and independent bookshops. A coffee at A Brasileira is a Lisbon ritual, though standing at the counter rather than sitting on a terrace reduces the price. Window shopping along Chiado’s streets is free, and the neighbourhood combines old-world elegance with contemporary culture.

In the afternoon, take an inexpensive bus or train to Alcântara to visit LX Factory, a revitalised industrial complex beneath the Ponte 25 de Abril bridge. Entry is free, and you can wander among street art, design shops, and second-hand stalls. Food trucks and casual eateries offer affordable lunches.

Return to the centre by sunset and make your way to Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara or Miradouro de Santa Catarina for panoramic evening views. End the day with grilled sardines or a bifana pork sandwich, accompanied by a glass of local wine, at a modest restaurant in Bairro Alto or Cais do Sodré.

Practical Budget Tips

Accommodation costs fall considerably if you stay in hostels, guesthouses, or private rooms in neighbourhoods such as Arroios, Intendente, or Graça rather than in the historic centre. Many museums are free on Sunday mornings or on the first Sunday of the month, so plan accordingly. Drinking tap water is safe, and filling a reusable bottle will save money. Finally, walking is often the best way to discover Lisbon; the hills may be steep, but each climb is rewarded with a new miradouro.

With thoughtful choices, two days in Lisbon can be both affordable and unforgettable.

Project Narrative: Documenting the Vanishing Industrial Corridor

Public libraries have long served as custodians of collective memory, yet the archival record remains conspicuously silent on the communities most vulnerable to economic and demographic change. [Library Name] proposes a twenty-four-month oral-history initiative to systematically record the experiences of residents, laborers, and small-business owners in the [Specific Area/Neighborhood] industrial corridor, a district now confronting rapid redevelopment and the displacement of multigenerational families. The project will produce a professionally archived, publicly accessible collection of first-person testimony that redresses a documented absence in the region’s historiography while reaffirming the library’s role as a nexus of civic inquiry.

The need for intervention is acute. Local archives and newspaper morgues catalog the institutional history of the area’s mills and foundries; they rarely preserve the quotidian textures of the neighborhoods that sustained them. As older residents relocate or age, and as new immigrant populations reshape the area’s social fabric, an unrecorded body of knowledge—encompassing shop-floor customs, entrepreneurial strategies, domestic practices, and interethnic solidarities—risks irretrievable loss. Preliminary reconnaissance conducted by library staff in partnership with [Local University] archivists confirms that fewer than a dozen extant interviews address the post-1960 period, and none foreground the voices of women, Indigenous migrants, or recent refugees. This project will fill that lacuna by conducting sixty full-length, filmed oral-history interviews, with deliberate attention to gender parity, linguistic diversity, and cross-generational perspective.

Methodologically, the program adheres to standards established by the Oral History Association and the Society of American Archivists. Participants will be identified through a network of trained community liaisons—faith leaders, union shop stewards, and ethnic association officers—rather than through open call alone, ensuring that recruitment reaches populations historically skeptical of institutional preservation efforts. Each narrator will participate in a pre-interview protocol to establish informed consent, negotiate archival embargoes, and map biographical themes. Interviews will be filmed in 4K resolution using broadcast-quality dual-system recording, transcribed to verbatim standards, and indexed using the Oral History Metadata Synchronizer (OHMS) to enable granular, keyword-level searching. Master files will be ingested into the library’s climate-controlled digital repository, with access copies hosted through a dedicated portal linked to the library’s main catalogue and, subsequently, the Digital Public Library of America.

The project does not treat preservation as an end in itself. A parallel public-history component will integrate collected testimony into the civic life of the city. Edited excerpts, vetted by narrators for contextual accuracy, will inform a rotating exhibition in the library’s main atrium and a companion podcast series distributed via municipal radio and streaming platforms. A moderated panel cycle—bringing narrators into direct dialogue with urban planners, labor historians, and policymakers—will situate individual memory within contemporary debates about displacement and economic rights. Finally, a curriculum toolkit derived from the collection, aligned with state social-studies standards, will be offered without fee to district high schools, ensuring that the archive functions as an active pedagogical resource rather than a static repository.

Sustainability will be embedded from inception. Partnership agreements with [Regional University] and the [Local Historical Society] guarantee post-grant archival hosting, ongoing metadata enhancement, and continued curatorial oversight. Graduate student archivists from the university’s public-history program will provide supervised labor, reducing per-interview costs while training a subsequent generation of practitioners in ethical fieldwork standards. Upon completion, the collection will constitute a permanent, open-access record—a counter-archive to the boosterish narratives of development that dominate municipal discourse.

In an era of accelerating demographic and technological change, the public library’s mandate extends beyond service provision to the rigorous stewardship of memory. This project asserts that ethically conducted oral history is not ancillary to the library’s mission but central to it: an act of civic documentation that honors the complexity of lives lived at the margins of the official record.

title: market research report|consumer demand for electric bicycles in Europe
text:
The European electric bicycle market has evolved from a niche segment into one of the most dynamic categories in personal mobility. Annual sales across the European Union, United Kingdom, and associated markets rose from under two million units in the mid-2010s to more than five million units at the 2022 peak, before softening somewhat in 2023 and 2024 as post-pandemic demand normalized and retailers worked through excess inventory. Germany remains the largest single market, with annual e-bike sales exceeding two million units at peak and e-bikes accounting for roughly half of all bicycle sales value. The Netherlands, France, Belgium, and Austria follow, with the Netherlands showing the highest per-capita penetration. Total market value is estimated in the range of twelve to fifteen billion euros annually.

Demand is underpinned by several structural drivers. Urban congestion and the reallocation of street space toward cycling have made e-bikes a practical commuting alternative, while municipal and national subsidies in France, Germany, Austria, and elsewhere have lowered effective purchase prices. Corporate leasing schemes, notably Germany's JobRad program and similar salary-sacrifice arrangements in the UK and Belgium, have expanded access significantly. High fuel prices, climate consciousness, and the pandemic-era preference for individual transport accelerated adoption, and continued improvements in battery energy density, motor weight, and integration have broadened the product's appeal.

The consumer base has widened considerably. Early adoption was concentrated among riders aged 55 and over seeking assistance on hills and longer recreational rides. That cohort remains important, particularly in the trekking and touring segments, but the fastest-growing group is now urban commuters aged 25 to 45. Electric mountain bikes represent a large share of sales in Germany and Austria, while classic city e-bikes dominate in the Netherlands and Denmark. Electric cargo bikes are a small but rapidly expanding segment, driven by young families in cities such as Copenhagen, Amsterdam, and Berlin, and by commercial last-mile logistics operators replacing vans. Speed pedelecs, which assist up to 45 km/h, remain a niche because they are classified as mopeds under EU rules, requiring registration, insurance, and helmets.

Regional variation is pronounced. Northern European markets are comparatively mature, with replacement purchases and upgrades forming a growing share of volume. France has shown the strongest recent growth among large markets, supported by generous purchase incentives and low-interest loan programs. Southern Europe remains underpenetrated, though tourism-related demand for e-bike rentals in Italy, Spain, and Portugal is building consumer familiarity. Eastern European markets are price-constrained but benefit from expanding local assembly and component manufacturing.

Average transaction prices typically range from 2,000 to 3,000 euros, with premium models exceeding 4,000 euros. Specialist bicycle dealers still account for the majority of sales, though direct-to-consumer brands gained share during the pandemic before facing a sharp correction; the 2023 bankruptcy of VanMoof and subsequent industry consolidation highlighted the risks of capital-intensive, inventory-heavy business models. Subscription and leasing services have emerged as an alternative for price-sensitive urban consumers.

Key challenges include the high upfront cost relative to conventional bicycles, theft and insurance concerns, regulatory fragmentation across member states, consumer anxiety over battery safety, and dependence on Asian supply chains for cells and drivetrain components. The 2023 to 2024 inventory glut forced heavy discounting and pressured margins across the value chain.

Looking ahead, most industry forecasts project mid-to-high single-digit annual growth through 2030. Structural factors remain favorable: cycling infrastructure investment continues, EU climate policy favors modal shift away from cars, and e-bike penetration relative to the total bicycle fleet remains low even in mature markets, indicating substantial headroom. Replacement demand, corporate fleet adoption, and growth in cargo and utility segments are expected to carry the market beyond its earlier peak, with sustainability of batteries and repairability increasingly shaping competitive positioning.

title: court opinion summary|a dispute over a contractor's failure to complete a home renovation
text:
COURT OF COMMON PLEAS OF SUMMIT COUNTY, OHIO  
MILLER, et al., Plaintiffs,  
v.  
HARRISON BUILDERS, LLC, Defendant.  
Case No. 2023-CV-01234

SUMMARY OPINION

This action arises from a residential home renovation contract. Plaintiffs James and Margaret Miller are the owners of a single-family residence in Bath Township. Defendant Harrison Builders, LLC, is a licensed general contractor. After the parties executed a written renovation agreement, the contractor abandoned the project before completion. The matter was tried to the court without a jury. The following opinion summarizes the court’s findings of fact, conclusions of law, and judgment.

Facts

On June 1, 2022, the parties entered into a fixed-price contract for the renovation of the Millers’ kitchen, master bathroom, and main-floor laundry room. The contract price was $85,000, with work to be substantially completed within ninety days. The agreement required progress payments at designated milestones and mandated written change orders for any alterations to the scope or price.

Harrison Builders began demolition in mid-June and received three progress payments totaling $57,000. By late August, only partial framing and rough plumbing had been completed. The contractor then demanded an additional $20,000 for allegedly unforeseen structural conditions, but it provided no documentation, no written change order, and no itemized explanation. The Millers refused to pay the extra amount until the contractor complied with the change-order provision. Harrison Builders stopped work in early September, removed its equipment, and informed the Millers that it would not return unless the $20,000 was paid in advance.

The Millers retained a replacement contractor to complete the project and correct defects in the partially completed work. The replacement work cost $102,000. The Millers sued for breach of contract, negligent misrepresentation, and a violation of the state consumer protection act, seeking $37,000 in excess completion costs, $10,000 for temporary housing, $5,000 for emotional distress, and attorney fees. Harrison Builders counterclaimed for $28,000 in unpaid invoices.

Issues

The principal issues before the court are whether Harrison Builders materially breached the renovation contract, what damages are recoverable by the Millers, and whether the contractor is entitled to any recovery on its counterclaim.

Analysis and Holding

A construction contract is subject to the ordinary principles of contract law. A party’s failure to perform its contractual duties without a legally sufficient excuse constitutes a breach. Where the failure goes to the essence of the contract, it is a material breach that excuses the non-breaching party from further performance.

Here, Harrison Builders abandoned the project before achieving substantial completion and demanded payment for unverified extras in violation of the written change-order clause. The contract did not permit the contractor to unilaterally increase the price or to suspend work for disputed change orders. Because the Millers’ refusal to pay the undocumented $20,000 demand was justified, the contractor’s abandonment was a material breach. The Millers were therefore excused from any further performance, including payment of the outstanding contract balance.

The proper measure of damages is the amount necessary to place the Millers in the position they would have occupied had the contract been fully performed. That amount is properly calculated as the reasonable cost of completion, less any unpaid portion of the original contract price. The replacement contractor’s charge of $102,000 was supported by itemized invoices and competent expert testimony and was reasonable under the circumstances. After subtracting the $28,000 balance still owed under the original contract, the Millers’ excess completion damages are $37,000. The court credits Harrison Builders with the value of certain materials left on site, reducing this award by $2,000.

The Millers’ claim for temporary housing expenses is denied. The record contains no evidence that the home was uninhabitable or that the Millers were required to relocate during the renovation. Their claim for emotional distress is also denied, as such damages are not recoverable for ordinary breach of contract absent egregious or extraordinary circumstances. The negligent misrepresentation claim fails because the pre-contract representations at issue were either statements of opinion or permissible sales talk rather than false statements of material fact. Finally, the consumer protection claim fails because there is no evidence that the contractor engaged in a deceptive act or practice at the time the contract was formed; mere nonperformance does not establish a violation.

With respect to the counterclaim, Harrison Builders is not entitled to the $28,000 unpaid balance because its material breach discharged the Millers’ duty to pay. Its alternative claim in quantum meruit is limited to the reasonable value of the benefit conferred. Given that much of the work performed was incomplete or required remediation, the court credits only $2,000 for usable materials delivered to the site.

Disposition

For the foregoing reasons, judgment is entered in favor of plaintiffs James and Margaret Miller against defendant Harrison Builders, LLC, in the net amount of $35,000, together with taxable costs. Defendant’s counterclaim is denied except to the extent reflected in the $2,000 offset already applied. Each party shall bear its own attorney fees unless otherwise provided by statute or contract.

It is so ordered.

title: encyclopedia article|the life and career of a nineteenth-century railway engineer
text:
Joseph Locke

Joseph Locke (9 August 1805 – 18 September 1860) was an English civil engineer whose surveys, earthworks and bridges helped turn Britain’s patchwork of local railways into a coherent national network. Born in Attercliffe, Sheffield, the son of a colliery viewer, he left school early to work in his father’s trade before joining George Stephenson’s engineering staff in 1823, aged seventeen.

His apprenticeship on the Stockton and Darlington Railway was brief; it was the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1824–30) that made his name. Working under Stephenson, Locke surveyed and supervised the northern half of the route, including the Olive Mount cutting, which ran for almost two miles through red sandstone and reached a depth of seventy feet, and the Sankey Viaduct, a 1,650-foot structure of nine fifty-foot arches crossing the Sankey Valley at a height of sixty feet. At the Rainhill locomotive trials in October 1829, he drove Stephenson’s *Rocket*, averaging 24 mph over the measured mile and touching a top speed of around 35 mph.

By the mid-1830s Locke had emerged from Stephenson’s shadow. Appointed engineer of the Grand Junction Railway in 1834, he rejected his former employer’s proposed route in favour of a more southerly alignment with easier gradients. The resulting 82-mile line from Birmingham to Warrington opened on 4 July 1837 and included the Dutton Viaduct, a 500-yard brick structure of twenty sixty-foot arches across the Weaver Valley. On this line Locke also promoted the use of double-headed rails in place of the fish-bellied rails then standard, arguing that they were easier to maintain and better suited to heavy main-line traffic.

In 1835 he became engineer of the Manchester and Birmingham Railway, opened in stages between 1840 and 1841. Under his direction, his assistant George W. Buck designed the Stockport Viaduct, completed in 1840: twenty-eight arches, 1,800 feet long and 111 feet above the Mersey, it was then the largest brick viaduct in Britain. Later commissions included the Lancaster and Carlisle Railway, opened in 1846, and the Caledonian Railway’s main line from Glasgow to Carlisle, opened on 15 February 1848, where gradients were kept to no steeper than 1 in 200 across the Southern Uplands.

Locke’s authority extended into public life. Elected Liberal Member of Parliament for Honiton in 1847, he held the seat until his death and served as President of the Institution of Civil Engineers from 1858 to 1859. He died on 18 September 1860 at Moccas Court, Herefordshire, aged fifty-five, and was buried in Brompton Cemetery, London.

At the height of his practice in the 1840s, Locke’s office was responsible for some of the most demanding railway projects in England and Scotland. His insistence on careful alignment, solid masonry and maintainable track laid down standards that shaped the main-line railways of Victorian Britain for decades.

title: encyclopedia article|the life and career of a nineteenth-century railway engineer
text:
Thomas Edmund Blackwell was born on 14 March 1811 in Newcastle upon Tyne, the second son of a colliery viewer and a schoolmistress. Displaying an early aptitude for mathematics and mechanics, he was articled at sixteen to a local civil engineer, where he gained practical experience in surveying and colliery railway work during the first widespread adoption of steam traction in the north of England. This apprenticeship coincided with the opening of the Stockton and Darlington Railway, an event that profoundly shaped his decision to specialize in railway engineering rather than follow his father into colliery management.

Following his training, Blackwell spent the mid-1830s as a resident engineer on the construction of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway's northern extensions, supervising embankments, cuttings, and the layout of intermediate stations. His competence in managing large navvy gangs and his innovative use of theodolite surveying in difficult terrain brought him to the attention of George Stephenson, for whom he briefly served as an assistant engineer in 1837. During this period, Blackwell refined his understanding of locomotive performance and track geometry, co-authoring a paper on optimal gradients for heavy mineral traffic that was read before the Institution of Civil Engineers in 1840 and later informed the alignment of several Pennine routes.

In 1843, Blackwell was appointed chief engineer of the Midland and Western Railway, a concern seeking to link the manufacturing towns of the English Midlands with the port of Bristol. Over the following fifteen years, he directed the construction of nearly two hundred miles of main line, including the celebrated Avonside Viaduct, a wrought-iron lattice structure spanning the River Avon that was among the longest of its kind when completed in 1851. He also supervised the difficult boring of the Cwmbran Tunnel through unstable shale, pioneering the use of compressed-air drilling machinery and timber shielding to reduce fatalities among the workforce—a method later widely adopted in Alpine tunneling across the Continent.

Blackwell's reputation for reliability and fiscal prudence led to commissions abroad. Between 1856 and 1864, he acted as consulting engineer to South American railway projects, advising on locomotive adhesion, rack-and-pinion systems, and trackbed specifications for high-altitude mountain railways in Peru and Chile. He subsequently declined a lucrative offer to oversee the Egyptian state railway, citing ethical concerns about the corvée labor employed on the project, a decision that earned him criticism from investors but enduring respect within the profession.

Returning to England in 1865, Blackwell entered into partnership with his eldest son, Robert, forming the firm Blackwell & Son, which specialized in railway dockyards and large interchange stations. He served as president of the Institution of Civil Engineers from 1871 to 1873, advocating for standardized rail gauges across British overseas possessions and for the universal adoption of interlocking safety signaling. His presidential address, "On the Moral and Material Responsibilities of the Engineer," remains a frequently cited document in the history of engineering ethics.

Blackwell formally retired from active practice in 1878, though he continued to serve as a Justice of the Peace and to contribute articles on bridge design to the technical press. He published a two-volume memoir, Tracks Across the Century, in 1884, offering a vivid firsthand account of the social and physical transformation of Britain by steam transport. He died at his home in Derbyshire on 22 November 1892, aged eighty-one, and was buried in the parish churchyard at Bakewell.

His legacy rests on the integration of mechanical ingenuity with a conscientious approach to worker welfare and public safety. Several of his major viaducts remain in use today on the national rail network, and the Blackwell Medal, established by the Institution of Civil Engineers in 1902, is awarded biennially for outstanding contributions to railway infrastructure design.

title: grant proposal|a community oral-history project for a public library
text:
Voices of Maplewood: A Community Oral History Project

Submitted by: Maplewood Public Library
Amount Requested: $24,500
Project Period: September 2025 through August 2026

Project Summary

The Maplewood Public Library respectfully requests $24,500 to support Voices of Maplewood, a twelve-month community oral history initiative. The project will document, preserve, and share the lived experiences of longtime residents, with particular attention to immigrant families, retired mill workers, and elders whose stories are largely absent from our existing local history collection. Trained staff and volunteers will record at least forty interviews, establish a freely accessible digital archive, and present public programs culminating in a community listening event and exhibition.

Statement of Need

Maplewood has changed dramatically over the past three decades. The closure of the textile mills, the arrival of new immigrant communities, and rapid redevelopment have transformed the town, yet the library's local history room holds mostly photographs and official documents, with few first-person accounts of these changes. Many potential narrators are over eighty years old, and the window for capturing their memories is closing. Oral history democratizes the historical record by including voices often excluded from official archives, and the public library, as a trusted and neutral institution, is the natural home for such a collection.

Goals and Objectives

The project pursues four goals. First, to record and permanently preserve at least forty oral history interviews representing the town's demographic and occupational diversity. Second, to build local capacity by training fifteen community volunteers in oral history methodology. Third, to foster intergenerational engagement by involving high school students as interviewers. Fourth, to ensure free public access to all recordings and transcripts through the library's website and listening stations in the local history room.

Methods and Activities

The project will follow best practices established by the Oral History Association. A part-time project coordinator will recruit and train volunteers in interviewing techniques, informed consent, audio recording, and transcription review. Each interview will be recorded in audio and video, transcribed, indexed, and archived with signed release forms. The library will partner with the Maplewood Senior Center, the Maplewood Historical Society, and Maplewood High School to identify narrators and recruit student participants. Public programs will include a panel discussion with narrators, a workshop on family oral history, and a final listening event with an accompanying exhibition of photographs and transcripts.

Timeline

Months one and two will be devoted to hiring the coordinator and training volunteers. Months three through eight will focus on conducting interviews. Months nine and ten will be dedicated to transcription, indexing, and archival processing. Months eleven and twelve will feature public programming, the community exhibition, and final evaluation and reporting.

Budget Summary

Funds requested total $24,500, allocated as follows: project coordinator stipend, $12,000; recording and listening equipment, $4,000; professional transcription services, $3,500; volunteer training led by a consulting oral historian, $2,500; archival storage and web hosting, $1,500; and public programming and exhibition materials, $1,000. The library will contribute staff time, cataloging support, meeting space, and promotional services as in-kind matching funds valued at approximately $6,000.

Evaluation

Success will be measured through quantitative indicators, including the number of interviews completed and archived, digital archive usage statistics, and program attendance, as well as qualitative feedback gathered through surveys of narrators, volunteers, and audience members. A final evaluation report will be submitted to the funder within sixty days of the project's conclusion.

Sustainability and Conclusion

The digital archive will be maintained within the library's existing systems at minimal ongoing cost, and the trained volunteer corps will allow the collection to grow well beyond the grant period. Voices of Maplewood will preserve irreplaceable community memories, strengthen bonds across generations and cultures, and affirm the library's role as the keeper of our shared local identity. We thank the committee for its consideration of this proposal.

title: court opinion summary|a dispute over a contractor's failure to complete a home renovation
text:
Hartwell v. Blackwood Contracting, LLC, Mass. Super. Ct., No. 1982-CV-00471 (DeLuca, J.) (Nov. 8, 2021).

In this residential construction dispute, the court found that contractor Marcus Blackwood, doing business as Blackwood Contracting, breached a written renovation agreement and violated G.L. c. 93A by abandoning a half-finished home renovation in Newburyport. Following a four-day bench trial, Judge Patricia A. DeLuca awarded homeowner Diane Hartwell $104,375 in damages, plus prejudgment interest and reasonable attorney fees.

The parties signed a fixed-price contract on March 15, 2019, for work at 14 Coral Street. Blackwood agreed to expand the kitchen, install white oak flooring throughout the first floor, and gut-renovate two bathrooms. The contract price was $187,500, with completion “substantially” required by June 15, 2019. Hartwell paid a $93,750 deposit on March 18 and a second draw of $46,875 on May 2, after demolition and rough framing were complete.

The project unraveled quickly. By late May, Blackwood’s crew had stopped appearing regularly. On June 3, 2019, Hartwell arrived at the house to find the front door unlocked, plumbing disconnected, the subfloor exposed in the kitchen, and a newly delivered vanity left in the driveway. Blackwood did not return calls or texts for ten days. On June 14, he emailed Hartwell stating that “material delays” made it impossible to finish on time and proposed a revised completion date of August 30. Hartwell rejected the proposal and terminated the contract the next day.

At trial, Blackwood argued that supply-chain delays excused the delay and that Hartwell had interfered by repeatedly changing paint colors and tile selections. The court rejected both defenses. The contract contained no force-majeure clause, and Blackwood produced no documentary evidence that ordered materials were unavailable in May or June 2019. As to Hartwell’s design choices, the record showed only two change orders—both signed by Blackwood and priced at $3,200, which Hartwell had paid promptly.

The court credited the testimony of Hartwell’s expert, Richard Silva of Silva Brothers Restoration, who inspected the property on June 22, 2019. Silva testified that the completed work was worth approximately $62,500 and that the remaining work, including correcting improperly sloped shower pans and reinstalling a load-bearing beam that Blackwood had notched, would cost $71,200. The court also found that Hartwell had spent $4,200 to secure the property and replace items stolen from the open jobsite.

Applying the Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 348, Judge DeLuca measured damages by the cost of completion, finding that figure more reliable than diminution in value because the defects were remediable and Hartwell promptly hired a qualified replacement. The damages calculation was: $71,200 (completion and repair), plus $4,200 (incidental expenses), minus the $11,875 credit representing the unpaid final contract draw. The court added $40,850 under c. 93A, finding Blackwood’s conduct—taking two-thirds of the contract price, abandoning the site, and falsely blaming the homeowner—was willful and knowing.

The court entered judgment for Hartwell in the total amount of $104,375, plus prejudgment interest from June 15, 2019, and directed the parties to submit fee affidavits within thirty days.

title: product review|a mid-range noise-cancelling headphone after three months of use
text:
Noise Cancellation in the Mid-Range: Three Months In

After roughly ninety days of daily use, the question is no longer whether these headphones cancel noise at all, but where, and how convincingly, they draw the line between silence and the world. Noise-cancelling headphones have become a category in which expectations are set by flagships that cost twice the price or more; a mid-range pair must be judged not by whether it matches them, but by how close it comes while avoiding the compromises that make everyday listening a chore.

The active noise cancellation here is at its best against low-frequency drones. On trains, the rumble of wheel on track subsides into a distant murmur; on buses, the engine note is tamed to something you notice only when a song ends. Aircraft cabins are the clearest win: the pressurized hum that makes long flights feel heavy is reduced enough that volume levels can stay low, which matters for fatigue over a four- or five-hour journey. It is not the eerie vacuum-seal effect produced by the best in the class, and an especially loud HVAC unit or a rattling window will still announce itself, but for the money the performance is credible and consistent.

Where the limitations appear is in the midrange and upper registers, which is to say the frequencies occupied by human voices, clattering keyboards, and crying children. The headphones dull these sounds rather than erase them. In a busy café, conversation remains intelligible; in an open-plan office, a colleague calling across a desk will cut through. This is typical of hybrid ANC at this price, and it is worth treating any marketing claim of “total immersion” with skepticism. What you get is a useful lowering of the ambient volume, not a private listening room.

The transparency, or ambient, mode is competent without being exceptional. Voices sound natural enough for brief exchanges, though there is a faint processed quality—like listening through a very good telephone line—that reminds you the microphones are doing the work. It is fine for ordering coffee or hearing a platform announcement; I would not rely on it for sustained conversation. Wind noise, too, is a weak point: walking along a breezy street with ANC engaged produces a flutter that becomes distracting enough that I usually paused playback or switched to ambient mode until I was under cover.

Call quality, often an afterthought on headphones in this bracket, is acceptable rather than impressive. The microphones pick up speech clearly in quiet rooms, but they struggle with background competition. On a windy corner or near roadworks, callers reported that my voice sounded compressed and occasionally clipped. For the occasional work call it is workable; for anyone intending to use them as a primary headset for remote meetings, it is a limitation to weigh.

The companion app adds value, mostly through a parametric equalizer and the ability to adjust the ANC intensity or switch between noise-cancelling and ambient modes. The EQ is genuinely useful: the default tuning leans slightly warm, and after some adjustment the headphones could be made to sound more even-handed, if still short of the detail and separation offered by wired competitors at the same price. Multipoint Bluetooth pairing proved reliable between a laptop and a phone, switching cleanly when a call came in, though occasionally the connection would need a manual nudge after waking from sleep.

Battery life has been the least contentious part of the experience. With ANC on, the claimed figure lands within an hour or two of reality after weeks of mixed use, and the quick-charge feature has bailed me out more than once. After three months there is no obvious degradation in runtime, though it is too early to make definitive claims about long-term cell health.

Taken together, the noise-cancelling performance is best understood as a practical convenience rather than a transformative technology. These headphones will not make a noisy train carriage disappear, but they will make it bearable, and they will do so without the flagship price tag. For the commuter, the occasional flyer, or the office worker who simply wants the background hum to recede, that may be exactly enough.
